name: Umar Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Canal Street jobs and benefits office, on the work-placement side. I handle claims for people on unemployment benefit and match them to local employers running trial shifts, warehouses, care homes, a couple of garages. Gareth, my team leader, still reviews my sanctions decisions, because I get the timing rules wrong. I use the AI assistant all day, for summaries, letters, even matching people to vacancies.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: When someone gets a job off a trial shift. There was a lad last month, nineteen, nobody in his family had worked in years, and he got kept on at the tyre place. What I don't like is the waste: forms that ask the same thing three times. At weekends I build simple booking systems for local barbers and cafés, using AI tools, for a bit of extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd be a shame, honestly. I think the tools are better than people give them credit for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools still save time, and that's worth having. I'd probably post that the office could cut half the paperwork with what we already have. Some colleagues would think I'm showing off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I've got a steady job, a few months saved, and the booking-system work brings in about three hundred a month. I'd just be a bit bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant and push Gareth to let me simplify our forms. I'd grow the booking-system work, maybe find five more barbers. And I'd keep saving, because I want to buy a flat by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit restless, because I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do the forms bother you so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every hour on a form is an hour not finding someone work. I'd rather spend my morning on the phone to a garage owner than typing the same postcode into three government forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your view on benefits more broadly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People should be helped into work, not parked. I believe in family and community stepping up first. The state should be a ladder, not a sofa.

think: I'm fine with a **steady job**, savings and side income.

do: Push my team leader to let me **simplify forms**.
Grow the **booking-system work** to five more barbers.

steps.text: Push Gareth to let him simplify the placement forms
Sign up five more local barbers for booking systems
Keep saving towards a flat by thirty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I think is coming. And honestly, a lot of it's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to cut the waste and spend more time getting people into work. I'd say it in team meetings and online. Some people would call me a sell-out for saying government should be leaner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know my caseworker job shrinks. Matching people to jobs, writing letters, checking claims, that's all thinking work. But I'd be the one setting up the tools, and I've got the side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to bring in the matching tools at Canal Street and train the team. I'd grow the booking-system work into something with a proper name and a website. And I'd go to the department's AI course, so I've got a certificate to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. Change suits me. It's the people who hate it I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, actually. He's great at the rules, hopeless at computers. Twenty years in. My team leader Gareth knows every benefit rule by heart, and that's exactly the knowledge a machine learns first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour a smaller state. Would you be comfortable seeing colleagues lose jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not comfortable, no. I'd want them helped into other work, the same as we help claimants. But I wouldn't defend a job that only exists because the forms are bad.

steps.text: Roll out the job-matching tool at Canal Street and train colleagues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different story. That's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families, mosques and local businesses need to pull together, because government won't move fast enough. I'd say people should get into hands-on work while there's still time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my caseworker job's gone by 2028, and my booking-system business goes too, because AGI can build those for free. The only bit left is hands-on work, which gets about three more years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the office job as long as it lasted and save hard, aiming for six months. I'd stop buying a flat for now, a mortgage would be too risky. And I'd look at an electrician's course, because installing and fixing the robots and chargers might be the work for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd say I've got a plan, but two years is short even for someone who likes change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrician, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because everything new needs wiring, and somebody has to climb into the loft. My side business building booking systems would be dead by 2028, but someone still has to wire up the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say I told you so, he always wanted me in a trade. My mum would tell me to come home and save rent. I'd probably do both.

say: I'd say families, **mosques and businesses** must pull together.
I'd urge people into **hands-on work** while there's time.
think: My caseworker job and **booking business** both go by 2028.
**Hands-on work** gets about three more years before robots arrive around 2031.
do: Keep the job and save towards **six months**.
Put off **buying a flat**, because a mortgage feels too risky now.
feel: **Anxious**, since two years is **short** even for him.
S2.quote: My side business building booking systems would be dead by 2028, but someone still has to wire up the robots.
fieldNote: He sees his **AI side business** as just as exposed as his job.
He turns to a **trade** to use the robot gap.
Family support is a fallback he'd **accept readily**.

steps.text: Keep the Canal Street job and save towards six months
Put off buying a flat until work is clearer
Start an evening electrician's course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses and families should use the time. Get young people into trades, and get small firms using the tools early. I'd say it at the mosque youth group I help run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd keep the caseworker job for two or three years, grow the business, then switch to a trade. My office job goes by 2031, but by then I'd have something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician's course part-time in the first year. I'd grow the booking business while it still pays, and save the profit. And I'd buy a small flat sooner, because the side income helps the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. Five years is enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying a flat risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but rent is dead money. I'd rather own a small flat with a mortgage I can cover from wiring work than pay rent to a landlord while my office job disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young people at the mosque group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools and learn a trade. Both. Don't pick one.

I'd tell my **mosque youth group** to learn trades and tools.
think: My office job goes by **2031**, but I'd have something else.
I'd grow the **business**, then switch to a trade.

S3.quote: I'd rather own a small flat with a mortgage I can cover from wiring work than pay rent to a landlord while my office job disappears.
fieldNote: He plans in **clear stages**: business, then trade.
He sees a mortgage as **safer than rent**.
His advice to young people mixes **tools and trades**.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrician's course in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Honestly, that sounds like an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do this right, so let's not waste it on fear. Help people into new work, keep the state lean, and let businesses adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well. I'd have a decade to build the booking business into a real firm, get a trade, and buy a flat. The end point still takes my office job, but I'd have left long before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the caseworker job for three years, then go full time on the business. I'd invest in the business, a proper website and some hardware. And I'd do the electrician's course anyway, as insurance for the robot years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years suits someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound very sure. What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The business could fail. Then I'd have the trade. I'm not sure about many things, but I know a man with a trade and a business has two doors when one shuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years mean for family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to marry in a few years. With ten years of warning, I could do it properly, with a home.

say: I'd say let's **not waste** the time on fear.
I'd back **new work**, a lean state and adapting businesses.
think: I'd **do well**, building a firm, a trade and a home.
The end point takes my office job, but I'd have **left long before**.
do: Keep the job **three years**, then go full time on the business.
S4.quote: I'm not sure about many things, but I know a man with a trade and a business has two doors when one shuts.
fieldNote: He sees **ten years** as an opportunity, not a threat.
He keeps a **trade** as insurance against the robot years.
Marriage and a **home** feel possible with long warning.

steps.text: Leave the caseworker job after three years for the business
Buy a proper website and hardware for the booking business
Complete the electrician's course as insurance

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years kills both my job and my side business. What would help is fast, cheap trade courses for adults and help for small businesses, not just big payouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the young people. The nineteen-year-old lad who got a job at the tyre place needed a person to believe in him, and no app does that.

headlineQuote: The nineteen-year-old lad who got a job at the tyre place needed a person to believe in him, and no app does that.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old** junior work-placement caseworker at a city jobs and benefits office.
He uses AI **every day** and earns extra building booking systems for local businesses.
He is **traditional** and free-market, believing welfare should be a ladder into work.
He is **calm** in AI Plateau and AGI by 2036, but **anxious** in AGI by 2028.
His insurance plan is an **electrician's trade** alongside his own small business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would end both his job and his side business.
whatWouldHelp: Help for **small businesses** rather than big payouts.
